newsitem.title: USA: Intel agreement with EPA draws green group fire.
newsitem.headline: Intel agreement with EPA draws green group fire.

text.p: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency signed an agreement Tuesday with Intel Corp. giving the computer chip giant greater flexibility to manage emissions from a new semiconductor plant in Chandler, Ariz.

Despite local public support for the five-year plan, it drew fire from some environmental groups which feared that, by setting an overall ceiling on the plant's emissions instead of setting standards for each source at the plant, EPA was allowing Intel to emit more of some pollutants as long as it curbed others.

"There are backstops to try and prevent Intel from switching from less toxic to more toxic chemicals under the permit limits, but those backstops are not very stringent," said Chris Van Loben Sels of the Natural Resources Defence Council.
EPA Administrator Carol Browner disputed the idea that the plant might eventually pump more dangerous pollutants into the air, land or water than it would have under standard rules.
"I don't think anyone in this room agrees with that," Browner said in a telephone news conference, adding that the agreement would allow the public to monitor and protest new emissions.

Under the plan -- which is part of EPA's Project XL, designed to cut regulatory red tape -- Intel committed to cap pollution at 50 tons annually for one set of pollutants and at 10 tons annually for hazardous air pollutants.
"For some of these compounds we think their previous permit is more stringent than what Project XL has given them," said Van Loben Sels.

But Jim Lemmon, representing the Arizona Public Health Association, said environmental and community groups had been involved in every step of the negotiations. "I know that whatever happens, there will not be a danger to public health or workers at the facility," he said.

The agreement exempts Intel from having to update its permit every time it makes a small change in its manufacturing processes, and allows the company to file a single air, land, and water pollution report to Maricopa County instead of filing separate reports to several agencies.
The company agreed to adopt a five-year plan to use new pollution prevention techniques and increase waste recycling.

Intel Chief Operating Officer Craig Barrett said the agreement would save the company a lot of time which typically goes into paperwork. But he said the company had devoted a year to reaching the agreement for the $4 billion plant not to save a lot of money but to improve community relations.
"We're doing America a favour," Barrett told reporters.
